England has to pay three-and-a•half millions

to pay? I see that some of the daily papers
suggest that a subscription should be started
by the guilty, headed by Mr. LAIRD, as the
most guilty, with a good fat proportion of the
profits which he made out of the Alabama.
This voluntary taxation of the guilty by
themselves, is, to say the least, very unlikely
to occur, a highly problematical solution of
the difficulty. The three-and-a-half millions

the question is who is to be taxed? I answer

taxed. Parliament, or Government, or the
governing classes, or all of these have some-

put this humiliation upon us. The working
classes, the poor, who have not made the mess

ment upon the upper and middle Classes, an

income tax or property tax. No doubt some

the three-and-a-half millions.

once to he up and doing, and make an effort

A CONSERVATIVE REPUBLIC.

M. TUIEILS has declared in his speeches and
addresses that the existing Government of
France is a Republic—only provisional it is
true, but which he expects to see firmly
established upon the dissolution of the present
Assembly, and the election of a new one: The
Times, however, in a number of its recent
leaders, expresses an opinion that the actual
Government of France is a personal one, and
not a Republic, of which l'sft, TITTERS is the
head; and that when a dissolution takes place,
the power of M. TILIERS will be greater than
ever.

f consider the writer of the article in the
:limes has made the miutake in confounding

the
..teieriti tiie power of M. TITTERS with real.
power, I. Tnrytas has, in reality, no power:

issiee coulld be, negatived, and rendered null
if the Majority of the Assembly chose. They.
allow hini togo on and have his own way, not
because either tho Monarchists or the Repub-
licans like M. TITTERS, or approve of his
measures, but because his resignation at: the
present time, before the war -Indemnity was
paidand the Trutsians leave Fritnei4.
throw everything into confusion, and might
cause a revolution and civil war. As soon, how-
ever, as the foreigner quitS the soil of France,
which will probably take place in less than six
months, there will be a dissolution and a new
thiimber elected, which will be at the same
time constituante and governing—that is to
say, Which will fix the constitution of France,
and govern the country at the Scalia time
according to the existing Provisional Republic,
Which places the full and entire power in the
hands of the National Assembly.
The Times intimates an opinion that the
new Assembly will _ consist of members de-
voted to M. TITTERS, who
.will thus become
more despotic than ever. In this opinion I
conceive the :Times is mistaken. That the
new Assembly will contain a great majority of
Conservative Republicans I have no doubt.
The addresses proceeding from the Councils
Generals sufficiently intinlate this. The ma-
jority of the Assembly, however, having the
voice of the country with them, will be per-
fectly independent, and will by no .means
allow U. TITTERS to have his own way, as the
majority of .the preepnt Assembly does, under
the fear of a dissolution. M. TITTERS is by no
means .a favourite with the Republicans,
although they have considered it their best
policy to support him at the present juncture
against the Monarchists. They consider
him—notwithstanding his undoubted talents
—an obstinate, bigotted old statesman. The
great majority of the Republicans are in
favour of Free Trade, as also of an Income
Tax, They likewise advocate the compulsory
recruitment of the Army such as exists in
Prussia. Those three great measures were op-
posed by M. TITTERS, and the Republicans
in the present Chamber were obliged to give
them -up in order to prevent M. TITTERS throw-
ing himself into the arms of the Monarchists.
By the resolution accepted by the ex-
isting Chamber, M. TITTERS was nominated
President or Prime Minister as long as the
present Assembly exists. As soon, however,
as a dissolution takes plane M. Timm is no

longer President. When the new Chambers
assemble a President will be appointed, and
in all probability M. Trtur.us will be re-
nominated. But he will only hold that office
as long as he gives satisfaction to the majority
of the Assembly. The very first questions
brought before the Chambers will in all prob-
ability be the abolition of the duties on raw
material, and the imposition of tin Income

Tax. The next will be the establishment of the
Prussian system of compulsory service in place
of the old practice of conscription—a substitution
which the Republicans have allowed M. TIITERS
to carry proviiionally, with the atyiere pensee
to change ell this as soon as they had the

power to do so. If M. TIMM does not give in
upon these poins, he will be dismissed, and
another President or Prime Minister appointed

T° probably Mr. GREVY, who although
_

not possessing:the talents of M. TIHERB ft

speaket, has infinitely greater common sense.
Such is the Conservative Republic of France
as it exists at present, and which we have no
reason to suppose the next Assembly will
modify or change in any respect. It differs
prinripie in a very slight degree from the
constitutional monarchy of England. In both
countries the supreme power exists in the
Assembly elected by the people. In England
it is the House of Commons which governs,
but not directly. For all its Acts require to
be sanctioned both by the Crown and the
House of Lords. The consequence is that the
will of the majority of a Liberal House of
Commons is frequently delayed, and some-
times even defeated by the passive resistance
of tho House of Lords or the intrigues of the
Court.

Whereas, in a Conservative Republic the
supreme power rrot only lies with the Assem-

,
bly, but that Assembly, elected by universal
eufrage, (Cots directly and immediately, with-
out consulting either lords or king. This is
real Parliamentary rule, real self-government,
or, ai the French term it, " Gouvernement
par le peuple at pour le peuple."

articles.text:
THE EARL OF ROSEBERY ON THE
AGRICUTURAL LABOURERS.

The Right Hon. the Earl of Rosebery was
presented with the freedom of South Queens-
ferry, near Edinburgh, on Saturday after-
noon, in presence of a large audience. In
acknowledging the honour which had been
conferred upon him, the noble Earl spoke at
some length. Having thanked the magistrates
and council of the town for their kindness, his
lordship proceeded to touch upon the question
of the agricultural labourer. In the course of
his remarks he said :—I think we must aid
acknowledge that the condition of the agri-
cultural labourer in parts of this kingdom has
been almost a reproach to our civilization. I-
will not identify what I say with any par-
tionlar place, but I do say there has been a
strange negligence of the interests of that
class. Various language has been used about
the (lotion they have now taken to improve
their position. One right rev. prelate said in
a post-prandial moment, that be should wish
the leaders of the Agricultural Union, if they
visited his neighbourhood, to visit a horse-
pond. (Laughter.) That was strong and
inadvisable language. I think he employed
it ivadvisedly, and that he has been rather
hardly used. He simply meant one of the
mildest pf jokes—laughter—and lie has been
taken up in a bloodthirsty sense; but that
should teach us to make an addition to a very
ordinary, proverb, "never to meddle with
edged tools," or with horse-ponds. (Laugh-
ter.) The disadvantages of meddling
with horseponds are two—the first is that
horsepond is not an argument that carries
permanent convictions to any minds whatever
'—(laughter)—and the second is that if you
once take to recommending horseponds as an
argument, and if the person to whom you re-
commend them happens subsequently to dis-
agree with you, he may remember your advice
—(laughter)—and put it in practice. against
yourself, and you may find it necessary to
make a personal experiment as to whether
truth lies at the bottom of a well or a horse.
pond. (Laughter.) aut the question is not
one to be treated with light words or with
horseponde. The agricultural labourers of this
country have formed themselves into a union.
It appears to me—l know it is not an opinion
which it universally held—that a union with-
in legitimate bounds, and governed on legiti-
mate principles, is a perfectly fair combination
for the defence or for the propagation of any
principles; and I do not think that any legiti-
mate objection can be taken to legitimate
agricultural Unions in defence of the interests
of labourers. When they come to strikes to
defend or better their position, the question
becomes an economic one. A strike, where it
is intended to raise the wages of labourers
above their legitiniate level as compared with
the price of other commodities, is economically
almstake. It would not take long to prove
that; nor would it take long to prove that if
you raise the price of labour you will have to
raise the price of all that sustains labour—the
food that is purchased by labour; and there-
fore the labourer whose wages are raised,
though he receives a larger amount of money,
will not, because he has to pay more for the
necessaries of life, have bettered his position.
(Applause.) .

HULL.
TERMINATION OF THE JOINERS' STRIKE.
The joiners' strike at Hull, which has lasted
13 weeks, has been brought to an amicable
termination. The wages of skilled workmen are
to be at the rate of 61d. per 'lour. The working
time is to be 53 hours for 40 weeks in the summer,
aad 47 hours for 12 weeks in the winter each year.
The won resume work at once.

PRESTON.
SitonT TIME IN THE COrrol

The apprehension mentioned last week respect-
ing the adoption of short time in the cotton
factories of Preston is already beginning to
assume a reality. On Saturday two of the largest
firms in the town, Messrs. Horrocks, Miller, and
Co., who employ between 3,000 and 4,000 hands.
and Messrs. J. Hawkins and Sons, who own five
or six mills in the town, gave notice of their inten-
tion to adopt short time. The hands employed by
the former firm will be put upon four days a week,
and it is probable that those of the latter will
work about the same nuthber of days. Other
millowners will, it ia thought, follow their ex-
ample. The high price of coal, mechanical and
other labour, and the uncertain state of tho cotton
trade are assigned as the chief reasons for the
change. The coming winter, it is feared, will be
a severe one for the operatives.

BIRMINGEAIt..
MEETING OF OPERATIVE JEWELLERS.

A general meeting of the above trade was held
at the Shakespeare's Head, ICenion-street, on
Wednesday evening; to take into consideration the
propriety of forming a trade society. Mr. Stephen
Green occupied the chair. There was a great
number of operatives present, and many were un-
able to obtain admission. The utmost enthusiasm
prevailed.
The Chairman said ho was surprised to find such
a large number of his fellow-workmen present.
They all knew that there had already been efforts
made to form a society. He believed the reason
that they had been unsuccessful was because they
had not been purely under working men's man-
agement. That meeting was simply a preliminary
one to bring a committee into existence, and their
time was very short. He supposed they would all
be favourable ,to the formation of a trades society.
(Hear, hear.)
Mr. Newcomb said that for a long time past the
masters had treated the men just as they thought
proper. He thought it was high time some
alteration was made. He should, therefore, pro-
pose the following resolution :—" That this
meeting having expressed the opinion that a trade
society should be formed, it be resolved that a
committee be formed from the company present,
and the business of that committee be to arrange
for the holding of a great meeting of the trade,
when resolutions of an important character should
be brought forward, and the meeting also pledges
itself to do all in its power to carry cut the object
in view." The speaker hoped the Loudon news-
papers would notice their effort so that the
operatives in the jewellery trade right through the
United Kingdom might hear of it, and join with
them. (Cheers.)
Mr. Stainton seconded the resolution. The jewel-
lery trade, he said, was very extensive. Other
trades had had the courage to start trades unions,
and why should , not they? He hoped all
present would employ their best eflbrts, ift order
that they might have as good a society as
other trades. The brassworkers and electro-
platers had only established their union a few
months ago, and now they were as strong as any
union need be. They did not want to strike, but
simply to bring about a unanimous opinion. The
chief thing they required was unity.. If one
branch of the trade should strike, let them all
assist; for then, and not till then, would they do
good.
The resolution was carried unanimously.
A committee was then formed from the mem-
bers present, for the purpose of carrying out the
wishes of the meeting. - - -

The officers elected pro. tem. were Mr. Stephen
Greene, Chairman; S. Stainton, Treasurer;
Francis Middleton, Secretary.
A considerable sum was collected for defraying
the expenses that would be incurred.

A vote of thanks to the Chairman brought the
proceedings to a close.

166, Brompton-road, Sept. Bth, 1872.
To the Right Rey. the Lord Bishop ot Gloucester

My Lord,—l hope you will pardon me for again
trespassing upon your valuable time, but being
assured, by your kind reply to my previous letter,
that you really have at heart the general welfare
of the agricultural labourer, I am anxious to lay
before your lordship's notice a few facts that have
come under my own observation.
As to the "labourers' claims being, for the most
part, fairly reconsidered by the farmers." Now
having gone thoroughly into the question of the
Labourers' Union, I am fully persuaded that
nothing else will move the firmers to meet the
said claims until it is generally established
throughout the country. I would here remark
that it it not the otatom t aATat the plus

where a meeting is to be held for subscriptions.
The 'Won is supported by the weekly subscrip-
tion of twopence from each member. Our sole
object is to raise the wages of the men to a fair
and just standard, and benefit the farmer by
avoiding strikes. Your lordship says that "the
farmers are slowly and kindly meeting their de-
mands," and that the farmers say "that they are
easing it to them, and are getting on capital on
both sides if the beggars outside would only hold
their peace." But as your lordship did not give
us the labourers' opinion upon the subject, I
thought I would just go down aid hear what the
men had to say. _ _

I accordingly started for North Leach, in Glou-
cestershire, accompanied by Messrs. Arch and
Taylor, and upon arrival engaged the town crier
to announce all day that the "beggars" were
come to town, which had the effect (being market
day) of bringing together the farmers of the place
In large numbers. Their statement was that their
men had about fifteen shillings per week with
perquisites, some they thought would soon have
to pay the income tax (?). I, of course, was de-
lighted to hear such good news, and the farmers,
in order to save us any trouble, wanted it to be
settled at that, and send us away. But as we had
gone to hear the men as well as the masters, we
sailed a meeting for the evening, and got together
about 600, and many farmers.
I announced to the men the above statement,
and how glad I was to find they were so well off.
When, to a man, they said it was not so.
I then asked the men—" What is the average
amount you earn per week ?" Ono and all
answered—" Ten shillings a week."
I then asked the farmers if that was true.
They held their peace.
I then asked the men if when they worked till
eight, nine, or ten o'clock, and sometimes later,
they received anything extra. They said no.

I then asked them if they lost time through
rain whether they were paid. About one-third
said yes, and the other two-thirds said no. (On
that same day, place, and county, a man was
tried before two magistrates, and convicted, for
refusing to work after seven o'clock, p.m.) Surely
the beat and fairest- way is to pay a man by the
hour. I speak from experience, and let the men
be paid for their labour in hard cash, in lieu of
cider.

Then as to conduct, I certainly wish I could
speak as highly of the language and actions of
the farmers, as I can of the men.
I have also found that the farmers strike their
average from casual men that only work for them
in hay or harvest time, and they do not earn more
than fourpence an hour, and often work eighteen
hours a day, and sleep in a barn or even in the
field. I do not think these men ought to be
reckoned with the farmers' men. Of course I have
found some very good men among the farmers,
but yet there is a deal to be done by some one to
raise the poor men from the generally miserable
and degraded position in which they have been so
long.
It has been said that an increase of wages will
lead to drunkenness, and the alehouse.keeper will
be the only one who will be benefited. There may be
such man here and there, but can we wonder at it,
when from boyhood they are taught by the farmers
to love strong drink. Well do I remember, when
a boy only eight years of age, I was sent into the
fields bird-keeping at 10d. a week and a pint of
cider a day. Who should have been blamed had
I grown up a drunkard? Depend upon it, my
lord, we have only to give the poor men a chance
of making home a little more comfortable, and bat
with few exceptions they will not wish to spend
their earnings either in ale or cider.
It is to be regretted that the public press is only
taking one side of the question. They seem to
refuse to take the part of the men, which makes
the battle harder to fight. But though might fre-
quently overcomes right, yet, "nil desperandurn "
is our motto, and we mean to press forward till
victory crown our efforts, and the hitherto neg-
lected and down-trodden English agricultural
labourer be raised socially, morally-, and spiritually
to the position he ought to occupy as a son of toil
and an Englishman.-1 have the honour to remain
your lot dship's most obedient servant,

articles.title: REPRESENTATION OF MORPETH AND THE COAL MINERS.
articles.text:
THE REPRESENTATION OF
MORPETH AND THE COAL
MINERS.

The pitmen have learned the lesson of the value
of agitation, and those who ran could read the
great yellow placards headed "Miners' Monster
Demonstration," which announced that an open-
air meeting would be held at Morpeth on Satur-
day, the 28th September, "for the purpose of
advocating the claims of the miners and working
classes generally to vote in local and Parlia-
mentary affairs." Then were set forth in con-
spicuous letters the sections of the respective Acts
under which those claims were advanced ; and
below, with a bold versatility there followed these
spirit-stirring lines
We take our stand on justice, and justice says to

That all mankind, both rich and poor, ought surely

to be free—
Ought surely to possess that right Kings eannol

take away,
That they should have the framing of the laws
which they obey.
Of this "Monster Demonstration," we give the
following :
The platform consisted of a lorry, with a few
chairs and table on the waggon-floor. It was an
effort of agility to get on the platform, and when
there the packing was found extremely close, so
that every now and then somebody dropped off the
edge into the dense crowd below. There were
about throe thousand persons present, and when a
big pitman with a " burr" that made the air
throb, rose to propose a chairman, the quiet hum
of conversation died away into a deep silence.
It was a town councillor of Morpeth who was
voted by acclamation into the chair. Ile took it
pro forma, rose, doffed his hat, which straightway
blow away into space, read with conscientious
minuteness the placard summoning the meeting,
and then proceeded to avow his sympathy with
the movement.

A colliery doctor then proceeded to address the
meeting. lie disobeyed the chairman by launch-
ing at once into personalities, and there was no-
thing worth noting in his speech. The doctor
was a fervent orator; his successor was—

A veritable pitman, a dry, quaint, sententious
speaker of great pith, combined with great oddity,
"One of the last things," so he began, "we seem
to lam n as human beeuns, is to grant joost the
saame prevlidge to oor fellow man as we enjye
oorselves." He spoke chiefly on the grievance of
withholding from the pitmen a voice in the
election of guardians, overseers, and local
" booards." "Now," he argued, "in this awd
and invalooablo country of oors—(grim laughter)
—we hay' many anomalies. A mail can be an
wi'oot any property qualillcation ; boot no
man can tak' his seat at baoard of guardians
wi'oot haavin a house mated at £25 a year.
Whoa is the workin' man so mated? The (Alyce
is sarourascribed, and the man elected knows little
or nowt aboot the poor. Do the guardians watch
over the poor or inquire into the sarcunastanc es of
applicants for relief? Noa, they laive them
things to relavin officer." ("No, no," by a voice
from behind.)

The next speaker was an Irish pitman named
Thomas Glassey, one of the originators of the
movement, and known to fain() as the "Chopping-
ton guide-post." lie was a fine, ardent young
fellow, with yellow hair, and a brogue broader

than the platform. His theme was the "political
emancipation of the miner and his direct repre-
sentation in the House of Commons." His speech
was in prose, but its gist is fully given in the lines
of verse of his own composition with which he
concluded. With flushed face, eyes flashing, lip
trembling by reason of the fervid depth of his
emotion, yet with voice sonorous and deliberate,
he rolled out the following lines :

Ye hardy sons of toil arise, ye Miners of the
North,
To claim the rights of labour, in your majesty

come forth;
Come forth, come forth in thousands, and let your

watchwo.rd be,
That you will not pause a moment in your struggle

to lie fret. _
In your struggle to possess what belongs to you
by birth,
As a portion of the nation, and as dwellers on the

earth;
Be faithful, never falter, in this truly noble cause,
And we'll win our rights as freemen for to make
our country's laws ;
To make these laws which others tee long have
made for you,
For too long we've borne submission the *many to

the few. -
Too long we have been divided, but now, my
friends, at length,
We've learned this useful lesson, that unity is
strength.
And now the trying hour is come, lot us united be,
To labour for this noble cause, and grand results
we'll see.

* * * * * * * *
We'll labour long and patiently, we'll labour one
and all,
To send a toiler like ourselves within St. Stephen's
Hall.
We'll try no more the wealthy, no more the
"Upper Ten,"
For what know they of the struggles or the wants
of lowly men.
What know they in their mansions, with their
princely halls and towers,
Of what thousands must put up with in a wee
bit cot like ours;
Where our parlour, and our kitchen, and our
sleeping room beside
Is a chamber, need I tell you, that is neither
long nor wide.
But can't we fled a toiler, a man of lowly birth,
A. one with scant possession of the good things of
the earth P
Who has toiled as we have toiled in a region far
away
From the fields and woods and flowers, and the
blessed light of day.
Who can rise and give expression in language
clear and strong.
To our hatred of oppression and every form of
tong.
Yes, we have found a Miner, a man of sense and
worth,
A one to nobly represent the Miners of the North.
Possessed of high intelligence, with culture much

refined, _
Whose
.labours in the past have been to elevate

mankind ;
To banish strikes for ever from every form of

trade,
Where they on peace and happiness have often

havoc nude. - __
Then let us pledge ourselves to-night to do

whate'er we can,
To send to famed St. Stephen's this true hearted

working man.

With a few more speeches and some formal re-
solutions the meeting terminated, and the assem-
blage broke up.
The man to whom the above verses refer as
having been chosen by the miners as their candi-
date in the event of their succeeding in being put
on the register, is Thomas Burt, a pitman for
many years, now secretary to the Northumberland
Miners' Association.

articles.title: TRADES UNION CONGRESS
articles.text:
THE TRADES UNION CONGRESS

The following Suggestions as a Basis for the
Standing Orders for future Trades Union Con-
gresses have been addressed by the Parliamentary
Committee to the Officers and Members of Trades
Societies and Trades Councils of the United King-
dom :--

GENTLEMEN,—Ono of the duties which devolved
upon us, as the Parliamentary Committee ap-
pointed at Nottingham in January last, was the
drawing up of Standing Orders for the better
despatch of business at all future Congresses.

In accordance with the instructions then received
we beg to lay before you the following suggestions,
earnestly requesting that trades societies and
trades councils, or the experienced officers and
members of trades anions, will favour us with
such additional suggestions as their judgment
approves for facilitating the transaction of business
at these annual gatherings.
It is necessary to be borne in mind that these

Congressess are essentially reserved for trade
union delegates, representing bona fide trades
societies, trades councils, and similar bodies, by
whatever name they may happen to call them-
selves ; and it is desirable that this fundamental
characteristic shall be retained.

The only latitude which the Committee recom-
mend is contained in No. 30, which gives the
power to invite persons, not delegates, to attend
the sittings of the Congress, and, it may be, to
speak, so that those who from time to time identify
themselves with the labour movement, whether in
or out of Parliament, may be able to be present
to give advice or aid in the great work to which
we have addressed ourselves.

With these limitations, which have become
expedient, not in an exclusive spirit, but in conse-
quence of the many important questions to which
we must from time to time devote our attention,
we believe that these annual Labour Parliaments
will matorially aid in giving tone and coherence
to the aspirations of our industrial life, and wiil
greatly, help us in getting such enabling laws
passed by the Legislature, as will be conducive to
the general welfare of the community, not of
sections only, but of all classes of our fellow-
countrymen.

We are, your obedient servants,

London.

articles.title: STANDING ORDEIO3.
articles.text:
STANDING ORDEIO3.

1. The Congress shall consist only of delegates
representing bona fide Trades Societies, and
Trades Councils, and similar bodies, by whatever
name they may, for the time being, be called.
2. Each delegate shall come provided with a
credential signed by the officers of the society or
council he represents, certifying to his appoint-
ment, such credential to be given up to the Secre-
tary, immediately on his arrival at the Con.
gross.
4. The time of meeting shall be as follows:
on the first day to assemble at 12 o'clock noon
prompt; on all other days at 9 30 a.m.; adjourn
at 1, re-assemble at 2, and adjourn at 5 o'clock
each day.
4. The roll shall be called promptly to time
morning and afternoon, the names of all dele-
gates late or absent to be read over with the
minutes each morning.

5. At the opening Of the annual Congress, the
Chairman of the Parliamentary Committee shall
take the chair pro forma until the Congress has
elected its own President.

6. A. committee of three shall be elected to
examine the credentials, and report Thereon to the
meeting.
7. The delegates shall then proceed to elect the
President of the Cengreas, preference being given
to a delegate of the town where the Congress is
being held.
S. The Congress shall then elect a Secretary, a
like preference being given.

9. The emigres shall then elect a vice-Presi-
dent, a door-keeper and a messenger.
10. A btanding committee of five shall then be
elected, to whom shall be remitted the whole
business of the Congress; the order of and subjects
for discussion, together with the whole financial
arrangements of the Congress. The vice-president
to be the chiiirman of the committee.
11. After the routine business of election of
officers and committee, the president shall formally
open the Congress with an address.

12. The standing committee, with a view to
securing a proper despatch of business, with perfect
fairness to all who have been to the trouble
to prepare papers, of which due notice has been
given, shall have power to divide the Congress
into sections, so that those specially interested in
any particular question may have the fullest
opportunity for its discussion.
13. The standing committee shall be allowed to
retire a 4 o'clock each day (one hour before
closing the sittings of Congress), for the purpose
of selecting and arranging the next day's pro-
gramme.

14. Each delegate shall pay to the treasurer, on
the first day of his arrival, the sum of 10s. towards
the expenses of the Congress; and in ease he
represents more than One society, 10s. for every

such society he is delegated to represent. The
names of those who have, and those who have not
paid, to be read over when the roll is called on the
following morning. No person shall be deemed a
member of Congress until his levy is paid.
15. The reader of a paper shall be allowed
twenty minutes; the mover of a resolution fifteen
minutes; succeeding speakers ten minutes each;
no one shall speak more than once on any one
question. After the reply, no one shall be allowed
to speak on the question before the chair, but it
shall be at once put to the vote by the chairman.
16. No second amendment, or rider to an on.
ginal proposition, shall be put to the vote until
the first amendment is disposed of.
17. The voting shall be by show of hands; but
in case of a dispute, the chairman may order a
division.

18. Two tellers shall be appointed by the Con-
gress, and their ruling shall be final.

19. If more than one amendment is proposed,
the standing committee may retire, together with
the movers of the resolution and amendments, for
the purpose of trying to secure unanimity, by
blending the amendments in such a manner as will
be most conducive to the harmony of Congress
and the despatch of business.
20. No delegate shall be allowed to read it
second paper until after all other papers, of which
notice has been previously given, have boon read,
unless by special permission and sisnotion of the
standing committee, and the formal consent of
Congress.

21. In the selection of papers to be read, pre-
ference shall be given to those of which notice has
been given, and in the order in which they have
been received by the committee.
22. Subjects having special reference to the
trade of the town or locality where the Congress
is being held, shall in no ease be allowed to oc-
cupy the time of more than one sitting of the
congress. And it is desirable that these special
subjects be laid before the committee as early as
practicable, for the purpose of arranging them
under one or two general heads, and embodying
them in one or two simple propositions.
23. No delegate shall leave the rem without
the consent of the Vice-President: and delegates
absent one whole sitting without leave of absence,
shall be named by the Chairman.
2.1, A General or Parliamentary Committee of
nine shall be elected on the last day of each Con-
gress, who shall continue in office until they
are re-elected, or their successors are appointed.
They shall elect from among themselves a
President, Treasure., and Secretary for the
ensuing year; and they also shall remain in
office until they are re-elected, or their successors
are appointed.
25. All surplus monies, after payment of the
expenses of the Congress, shall be handed over to
the Treasmer of the Parliamentary Committee for
the general purposes of such Committee.
26. The duties of the Parliamentary Com-
mittee shall be (1) to watch
,all legislative
measures directly affecting the questions of labour,
and (2) to initiate, whenever necessary, such
legislative action as Congress may direct, or as the
exigencies of the time and cireumstauces may
,
demand.

27. The officers, under the direction of the
committee, shall have authority to solicit sub-
scriptions, donations, or levies, for the purpose of
defraying the expenses incurred by such com-
mittee; but the mode of payment shall be left
optional with each society as to whether it shall
pay by levy or donation.

articles.text:
" AIILD LANG SYNE."

"Far from the busy hum of men," two little
tillages were dotted down, one in the county of
Gloucestershire, the other separated only by the
River Thames, in Oxfordshire.
The Gloucestershire village is called Long
Hampton, the other Little Hampton.
Between these two villages, from time imme-
morial, has existed a rivalry. The Long Hamp-
ton and the Little Hampton cricket matches have
always been with the neighbourhood subjects of
Intense interest. But for several years Long
Hampton has been triumphant, and that, mainly
owing to the skill and spirit of two brothers, Jack
Wad George Hazel. They were the life and soul
of all that was going on in Long Hampton. In
mummer the Long Hampton cricket club flourished,
and victoriously the chosen eleven of the Glou-
cestershire village carried all before it. In winter,
none woo readier than Jack and George Hazel,
either in earth-stopping to provide sport for the
hounds, or (especially at Christmas time), by
gifts of coals, meat, and money, to lighten the
burden of poverty and old ago.
Many a weary old man, weary :from a life of
toil and an old age of poverty, had cause to bless
the warm-hearted charity of the 'brothers.
• "God bless 'em—they're just like their dad."
No greater praise could be bestowed; at least, so
thought the simple-minded inhabitants of Long
Hampton, for the father of Jack and George
liazelhad lived a simple and frugal man, whereas,
had he so have chosen, he:might have been a proud
and opulent one. But John Hazel, the elder,
chose rather to live poor, die poor,leaving to his
sons in place of amassed wealth, only the freehold
farm of two hundred acres, and the " God speed
you," of everybody. Nor did the brothers, after

their father's death, disappoint the hopes of their
neighbours, who, lamenting the old man, yearned
to sea his sons walk in his steps.
They were "chips of the old block "—generous,
honest, brave—so said all Long Hampton.
sack and George were twenty-four and twenty
when they followed their father to his gra ye in
the quiet old corner of the churchyard, where, for
more than two hundred years, the Hazels had
laid their bones.
Brought up together as children, having lost
their mother before memory began, they had
played, fished, birds-nested, erieketed together in
Ow sunny summer 6m,1 and in winter their
games and sports, whether snowballing, skating,
sliding, sparrow-netting or what not, were always
shared in common.
Then when the two boys were sent:to school, it
was grand to see how they stuck together; how
the elder, Jack, thrashed, or tried to thrash, all
the big boys who lashed his younger brother, and
how the younger brother took many lickings
rOlkey than get Jack in a fight in which he, Wee
tct bp worsted.
And so all went on smoothly until at the date
'Then our dory begins. Jack was twenty-laic, and
Qeorge twenty-two. Their father had been deal
two years, and the brothers farmed the two
hundred acrey, And were as happy as the day is
long.

The farm wap aituated, as we have said, on the
has of the ieje, which divided alike the counties

• We shall be glad te receive original coznpositions trora
our oubscribere to till this " place of lionour.**

of Gloucester and Oxford, and the villages of Long
and Little Irampton. The grounds of the house
of Moreton MArsh farm ran down to the river,
where a boat-house and punt gave ready access
to the other 'shard and 'county. 'Now; the land on
the other side belonged to one Owen Meredith, an
old man with one daughter. He was, so people
said, a rich man, but had he not a stiver in the
world, he would still have been rich with such
girl as Myra Meredith to call him father. Myra,
at this time, was seventeen—handsome, loving,
gentle, and good. There was but a stream divid-
ing the two farms, and seeing each other every
day, it would have been strange indeed had not
one of the ;,brothers, fell in love with the gentle
Myra.

Jack and George were in:temperament different
as light from darkness. Jack—quiet, reserved,
almost shy; George—dashing, impetuous, the life
and soul of everything, quite a rustle Prince Ru-
pert. With the great majority, the light-hearted
George was the favourite, but the great majority
did not, at the time, appreciate the quiet, earnest
nature of John. They were so accustomed to his
kind, quiet manner, and took it as much a matter
of course •as they would the light of the sun.
George, on the other hand, was never the same
—all life, spirits, .and energy; he seemed lake a
comet or shooting star, and perpetually claimed
their attention. John, as the elder, exercised a
great influence over George. He stood in place of
father and mother to him, and no spoiled child was
ever so watched over as George Hazel by the quiet,
reserved Jack.

Both were tall and handsome, but George, the
younger, was fair, and had blue eyes, and a
woman's dancing smile, while Jack was darker,
graver, and altogether more staid and quiet.
Jack, the elder, had always given way to his
younger brother, both in trifles and in more impor-
tant matters. George, on his part, could not but
be deeply sensible dills elder brother's unvarying
kindness, which:had flowed on in a steady stream
from the far back days of childhood. Ire loved,
and what is more, respected his calm, grave
brother, who laughed at his fun, smiled at his
follies, and scarcely reproved his faults.
Surely, one would think that oven the enemy of
mankind would fail in paking enemies of those
two •

And yet it was to be. John"nnd George Hazel
are destined to part as deadly enemies—aye I
worse, for an old enemy may become a firm friend,
but an old friend, once estranged, is usually an
enemy to the last.
Myra Meredith had an only brother Philip,
who, in every respect, was what a son and brother
should be.

Philip Meredith and John Hazel were fast
friends. Phil, indeed, was Jack's only intimate
friend, for his reserved. nature did not invite
familiar friendship, though his character and ster-
ling qualities commanded universal respect.
Philip was passionately fond of his beautiful
sister Myra, and although, perhaps, he would
rather have seen her give the preference to John
Hazel, yet next to his friend, that friend's brother
was the man he would have chosen for his sister's
future husband.

The summer passed quietly on. Sunny June,
sultry July, and August came and went, and the
yellow tinge in the corn told of the near approach
of harvest. Nearly every evening, when the
labours and joys of the day were over, the two
brothers would go down to the boat-house, ferry
themselves across, and stroll up to Ladygrove, as
the farm of Owen Meredith was named. The old
man was antiquated in his habits, and adhered
both to the dress and habits of a past generation.
His knee-breeches and drab gaiters, replaced when
ha went out in the fields by Jelin Ball top-boots,
were, but the outer signs of the old man's inner
life. Living in the days of steam and telegraphs,
he could not forget the olden times of mail coaches
and couriers.

Owen Meredith loved the old hall of the farm-
house, with its enormous firo-place and ancient
chimney-corners ; nor could anything induce him
to sit in the parlour, a room on the decoration of
which Myra had exhausted her various tastes and
ingenuity.

The old farmer's great delight was a game of
cribbage, and in this John Hazel never failed him.
As regularly as the sun went down (except on a
special occasion, such as a cricketing supper), John
Hazel would obtain the cards and board from Myra,
and, carrying a small table to the chimney-corner,
would play the best out of five games with Owen
Meredith. They played for half-a-crown a gone,
and though, during the last three years, some
thousanfis of games bad been lost and won, yet
there was not, between the two, 4 difference of
twenty half-crowns; so, on the whole, it WAS a
very harmleas amusement.
While John and the old man fought over their

game, Myra and thorge usually held 'a
quiet tete
ri tete by the window, and Philip, who was
musically inclined, would take down his flute, and,
seating himself in the perch outside, would pine
away to the great amusement of the swallows
under the eaves. At ten o'clock supper would be
placed on the table, and shortly after Jack and
George would say good night, Philip and Myra
sometimes walking with them down to the river,
which divided Long from Little Hampton.
And in this quiet manner, varied only by an oc-
casional cricket match, regatta, or country festivity
called "feast," the summer slipped on, and
autumn, with its rich harvest of fruit and grain,
arrived,

But while yet the corn sheaves were not all
stacked, and ore the flight of the swallow and fall
of the yellow leaf, there was an arrival in the
neighbourhood. The great house at Long Hampton
had been long untenanted. Squire Vernon had
resided abroad with his only daughter, Viviana,
for nearly twenty years. A straitenod income and
heavy encumbrances on the estate necessitated
this course; but now, after some eighteen years of
exile, the squire had so far righted himself as once
again to be able to take up his abode in the home
of his ancestors—Long Hampton Hall.
He was warmly welcomed to the old place, for
there were many yet alive who could remember
the family before adversity and misfortune had
driven them away. But though after his long
exile Squire Vernon was now able to resume his
ancestral seat, he was still a poor man; and, in
place of the grand carriages and profuse hospitality
of his predecessors, a saddle-horse for himself and
daughter, a pony-chaise and dog-cart with some
five servants only, were all the establishment at
Long Hampton Hall.
It chanced, some weeks after their arrival, that
John, who was a great fisherman, the solitude and
quiet of that pursuit according wal with his
nature, was trolling in the punt for pike, which
abounded in the stream. Hearing a splashing in
the river above him, he looked around, with
some annoyance, to see what it was which thus
threatened his hopes of sport, and saw a small
skiff floating down the stream, in which was seated
a young lady. As the skiff came nearer he noticed
that the young lady was very handsome, and also
that she had lost one of the sculls, which she was
vainly endeavouring to regain by means of the
remaining one,

" Sir, will you kindly oblige me by getting tbe
oar 1 have lost? I am afraid I have disturbed
your sport, but indeed it was unintentionai."
She spoke in the sweeteat of voices, and with a
slight foreign accent, which was perfectly charm-
ing.

John Hazel gladly complied, and when be found
that the young lady was quite ignorant of boating,
.he offered to row her boat to where she wished.
Not without some little hesitation this offer was
accepted; and, first fastening up the punt in the
boathouse, he took the sculls, and in a very few
minutes rowed the young lady to the landing
stage on the grounds of Long Hampton Hall,
which, like Moreton Marsh Farm, ran down to the
river. The young lady thanked him with a bright
smile, and ran off towards the house. John at
oneo judged rightly that this could Le no other
than the daughter of Squire Vernon. As he
walked slowly back he could not help reflecting on
her great beauty and charming piquant manner.
Now John Hazel was, or affected to be, indif-
ferent to women, and often said that he would live
and die a bachelor. George would marry, and one
woman in the old farm-house would be quite
enough. Philip Meredith, bo, Lacked up his
friend in his resolve, and declared his intention to
do likewise. John Hazel was always a great
fisherman, but even Philip could not quite account
for the enthusiasm with which he followed the
sport this autumn—an enthusiasm which, strang o
to say, met with but poor reward, for he returned
day after day sometimes with an empty basket,
never with a filled one.

"George, just go round the field to-clay and
send that wheat to market. I think I shall go pp
the stream and kill a fish or two."

Snell like speeches were now frequent with the
ehler brother, and the younger always laughingly
agreed, though ho could not quite make out the
extreme ardour with which John pursued the

angling art.
As the reader may have guessed, however,
Vivinna Vernon had more to do with these after-
noon fishings than either pike or perch. Strangely
enough, John Hazel was continually meeting the
young lady, who, on her part, was continually
getting into some little difficulty Nat which be
was in politeness bound to extricate her. Then,
when they became a little better iv:painted, she
actually begged him to teach her to row. How
could he refuse ?

ting an end to John Hazel's fishing and Vivitines.
boating lessons. But though winter could do this,
all the ire, storms, snows, and frosts could net,
quench the fire which had begun to burn in the
honest heirt of John Hazel, nor could it prevent
the young lady from taking solitary rambles, in
the course of which she sometimes (accidentally 1)
met the young farmer.
Quiet and reserved outwardly, there was•
A
world of Power in John Hazel which carried all
before it; and, long before the blossoms d'aiiiing)
Viviana Vernon, notwithstanding that her fathef ,
was as poor as proud, had vowed her love for
and had pledged herself to obtain her fathe.rt,
consent.
Nor did she fail in her promise. Petted and
spoiled al her: life, she, boldly went to proud
Squire 'Vernon and told him plainly that she loved
John Hazel, and asked his consent to their
marriage.
The old Squiro was aghast, breathless with
dismay, but he loved his daughter, and wilt 4 is
more, he knew her wild impetuous nature, and.i
fond father as he was, pocketed his pride, ftna
made her happy by giving his consent, after due
inquiry as to tile character and circumstances of
John Hazel.

Great was the astonishment in Long littroPtoll
when it was noised about that quiet John Ira
had won the Squire's beautiful daughter, and
would wed her in the autumn. Prodigious was
the joy among the neighbours, and many declared,
after mature thought, that of the two, Squire
Vernon received the greatest honour, so great
were John's sterling qualities and earnestness of
disposition appreciated.

As for the successful lover, he took the jokee
and chair of his brother and Philip all in good
part, willingly and without replying, and it was
finally arran.,ed that George should marry Myra
Meredith, at the same time that Sohn married :
Viviana Vernon. He steadily refused the Squire's
offer to take up his abode at the hall after his
marriAge, and declared respectfully, but firmly',
that his own home, humble as it was, was the
place for his wife, and in this Viviana willinglY
agreed.
Hitherto Georgo Hazel had seen little or
nothing of Miss Vernon, but when the engago,.
ment was public and sanctioned by the Sqniref
she was a constant visitor at Moreton Marsh.
George Hazel was at once struck with her ,
beauty, her fatal beauty, and, almost before he
knew what he was doing, was head over ears in
love with his brother's betrothed. Spoiled
and petted all his life, his every wish and whim
gratified by that brother, George did not strive
against this criminal passion ; but gave way to
the madness with all the vehemence of his fin'
petuous nature.

John Hazel dreamed not of danger, or he would
have removed his future wife from the chance of
danger; but his mild nature was incapable of
suspicion, and to suspect his own brother of such
baseness was to him impossible. ' The spring, .
passed and the summer came. John Hazel 514 -1
with pleasure that Viviana favourably impressed'
his brother, and was grateful for the attention he
bestowed on her, never dreaming of danger.
Viviana was at first amused by the high spirit/
and dashing manner of the younger brother, and
did not fear for her heart's allegiance. But the
very vehemence of George's nature, his handout°
face, sparkling blue eyes, his high spirits, and her •
own fickleness, at last prevailed over her sense of
honour and truth, and even the real love she bore
John. She persuaded herself, at first, it was hut*
flirtation, and laughingly listened to the impne*
sioned speeches of the younger brother.
But in time a species of infatuation posses&
her. She did not really love George, but if she
could have analyzed her own heart, she would
have known that his brilliant powers, high
spirits, and impetuosity had dazzled her imagina-
tion. John Hazel could have saved her at ani
time, but be dreamed not of danger, aed 13ever
thought to receive so fatal a stab from a brotherie

It is July, and the marriage i are to take

the gentle Myra, as formerly,
but in the

it, either by the sweet girl herself, or even her
brother. George volunteered to take Viviana for
a row up the river, as John was out in the field;
then she could return to tea at the Marsh. While
they were gone John Hazel returned, and finding
no one at home took his fishing-rod; intending t°

A favourite place was by the side of the boat-

song of the blackbird.
John listened to the conversation of the pair,
at first with amusement, then with astonishment,
and then his cheek grew deadly pale.
Could he be mistaken P Was his own brother

A Highland piper, having a scholar to teach,
disdained to crack his brains with the names of

Here Donald," said he, " tak' yer pipes, lad, and

articles.text:
HOW OUR ANCESTORS BRIBED
ELECTORS.

There is a variety most creditable to English
invention in the way in which our ancestors ad-
ministered their bribes. At one place a mysterious
person used to arrive with the cash, known as the
'Man in the Moon," who aPpronohed at nightfall,
and was at once met with, What news from the
moon ?" This was a poetic form. Then there
was the humorous form. "I'll lay you five
guineas," said a celebrated canvasser in Fox's
contest of 1784, "and stake the money in your
own hands, that you will not vote for Mr. Pox."
" Done!" says the free and independent, and wills
Itia bet and bribe. Another playful plan was to
buy the elector's canary at a price that would have
been handsome for a bird of Paradise—a very
pretty kind of bird fancying! Sometimes men
Showed perfect genius in availing themselves of
professional advantages. Thus a military gen-
tleman employed in the recruiting service once
Stood for Great Grimsby, and enlisted a majority
of the voters for soldiers with a liberal bounty!
EXCELLENCE IS WHAT PAYS BEST.
