THE RELIGIOUS EQUALITY CRY.
THE "advanced" section of the Liberal
party have chosen their cry for the coming
session; or at least it has been chosen for
them by those who constitute, in a great mea-
sure, their thew and sinew. That cry is to be
for absolute religious equality before the Igor.
Will this programme be accepted by these
who were not, and could not, be present at

Its formal adoption? Will it be accepted, for
example, by the working men ? We are not
prepared to answer this question with an un-
qualified affirmation. We have no doubt that
the proposed cry will be accepted by such
working men as have studied the question in-
volved with free and unprepossessed minds;
but there yet remain outside of these a vast
number of honest men who either have not
gone deeply into the matter, or are preoccu-
pied with other questions, the appeal of which
comes more home to their own business and
bosom, or who, by habit and association, stand
in such relations to the State establishments
of religion which would have to fall should
the contemplated cry prevail ;• as, for the
present at least, incline them to look with
aversion, suspicion, or neglect, on all propo-
gals of the kind that are displeasing to those
reverend and affluent persons among whom
the privileged churches find their staunchest
supporters.

We are here alluding to the Conference just
held in Birmingham. When we state that in
the Conference itself, at the dinner which
followed, and at the vast public meeting in the
evening, Mr. EDWARD Mum. was the prin-
cipal object of attraction, it will be well
understood of what kind of materials the
assemblies wore composed. That gentleman
was received all the day through with a
unanimity of enthusiasm which implies at
once admiration of the course which he has
thus far pursued, and confidence in his leader-
ship to the end, with perhaps a persuasion and
expectation of his full, his complete success.
We know of no public question, of no col-
lective forms and shapes of public opinion,
which exceed, or even come up to that
question wherewith the independent mem.
her for Bradford has identified his name,
character, and life, and to those assemblies
periodical or occasional in which he appears as
the central figure, in that union of intellect and
heart, of conviction and earnestness, which, in
all really great matters, constitutes the soul
and pledge of eventual success. It is not
flattery of the man, nor is it any desire to
place very prominently the possession of one
personal leader as the greatest thing of all,
that makes us say this. That Mr. MIALL has
come to be the acknowledged master of a
certain school of thotight, cannot be blinked;
but ho would be first to admit, and would
glory in the admission, that he owes the great
way he has made to the excellence of the
material on which he had to work.

The men who met in Birmingham disclaim,
indeed, the notion that they are to be regarded
in the light of Nonconformists. Not, how-
ever, that they are not, in the main, of that
character; but, that, from this time forth, as
to dealing with publics questions, they are
determined to merge it in the wider character
of patriots, Liberals if, you will, in short,
Britons. The Protestant Dissenters of England
and Wales were always a strong and :respeotable
body, but they were not always so strong as of
late years they have become. They came of
a strong ancestry, the old Puritans; men of
conscience, and ready to suffer anything for its
sake; men of pure and holy lives, every one
L saint and a hero; men or eminent mind
and learning, and qualified to meet any comer
in the intellectual field. These characteristics
descended from generation to goneration,:from
before the Commonwealth till after the Revolu-
tion. Nor were they over satisfied with that
" toleration " which came in with WILLIAM of
Orange, and was perpetuated under the House
of Hanover. With that condition, however,
they were so far content that all those who,
from time to time, attempted to bring them
back to their own root principles, and to rouse
them to a determination to insist upon full
religious liberty, found themselves overtasked,
and counteracted by the sluggish feeling of
the period, and by the insinuations of an
effeminate sentiment which set religion at
variance with politics, as though to meddle
with publio matters had been to imperil the
soul. Mr. EDWARD MIALL owes his eminence to
the fact, that it was given to him, after suffer-
ing much misconception and even obloquy
among his own people, to raise the Dissenting
mind and breast above all this, and to inspire
myriads of young men with the conviction that
it was their very highest religious duty among

men to contend for the entire liberation of
religion from State patronage and control, and
to make all men and all sects of religionists
perfectly and absolutely equal in the eye of the
law.

Such, then, are the materials which com-
pose, in great measure, the advanced section
of the Liberal party, a mass of mind and of
heart, which, for the harvest it promises, may
be regarded as so much virgin soil scarcely yet
touched by spade, plough, or harrow. Now,
from the moment that these men merge
their Noneonformist character in that of citizen
they naturally and necessarily come to the
front of the Liberal party in political affairs.
Not that they for themselves, or we for them,
claim any special leadership; but that, from
the very breadth and depth of their princi-
ples, which, though heretofore applied and
perhaps confined to religious matters, are, in
their own nature, universal and universally
applicable. In fact they specially are very
much in the same predicament with many
others besides of being quite willing to go on
with our institutions as they now stand so long
as they will answer the purpose, yet quite
ready to go the whole length of their principles
both constitutionally and in practical applica-
tion when the time,'if ever, shall arrive. In
short, they look extremely like the natural
leaders of the people if the people will have
them.

Everything does not depend upon the pre-
sent Ministers of the Crown. GOD help both
Crown and country if it did I Nevertheless a
great deal in the immediate future does de-
pend upon the course which our present rulers
shall pursue. They will not meet Parliament
next year in exactly the same personal com-
position as they parted from it in August.
There will be a different Lord Chancellor
for instance. A better, in some respects, could
hardly be; one more solid, even as a lawyer,
and more brilliant, as a debater, has probably
been found ; one, too, which is snore difficult
perhaps equal as a man. But between Lord
ITATITERLEY and Sir ROUNDELL PALMED., as
political thinkers, there is a palpable, a wide
difference. A Radical Chancellor was one
thing; a Conservative-Liberal one will be
another. As it was, the Radical element, in-
fused by Mr. GLADSTONE into his Cabinet,
could not well, after Mr. l3nianT left, maintain
itself in any potency against those elements
which came from an opposite quarter. Mr.
WINTERBOTHAM is but a " humble " member
of the Administration. Mr. STANSFELD, who
has reached the higher grade, once met on
the same thorough-going committees with Mr.
Mull, and may prove staunch. Yet after
the open retrogression of a Radical, at first so
fair in seeming as Mr. FonsTEn, we must b e
prepared for anything of the same- kind,
particularly if the admirable lawyer who de-
clined the woolsack because ho could not
consent to the disestablishmeut of the Church
in Ireland, should turn out to have now
accepted it on explanations as to the future
reconcilable to his upright but none the less
prepossessed mind.
It cannot but be perceived, therefore, that
this Birmingham Conference has taken place
at a delicate conjuncture, and that the
decisions which it has announced will have,
and ought to have, all the more weight on that
account in the public mind. What are these
decisions? The principle of religious equality
having been partially adopted in acts of
the Legislature, its complete application, to
the Established Churches of England and
Scotland, is forced upon public attention. In
view of this irrefutable statement,the Conference
heartily approves of the " decisive" terms of
the motion of which Mr. Mum'. gave notice for
the coming session, and it calls upon those who
Will listen to its voice, to spend the interval in
diffusing information, in promoting petitions
to Parliament, in organising themselves in
their districts, and, above all, in making wise
and early preparation for the next general
election. In addition to these purely practical
points, the Conference, in a separate resolu-
tion, touched two others of the highest moral
moment and. force ; first, the BENNETT
Judgment, as injurious to the interests of
religious truth in the Church, and as an addi-
tional injustice inflicted upon all outside its
pale ; and, secondly, the right of self-govern-

ment, as inherent in the idea of a Christian
church, and indispensable to the free and full
development of its spiritual power.
The latter of these lies in a well so deep that
he who would get at it must have something to
draw with. The former is obvious enough in
both its branches. But the practical question,
especially that of preparation for the first
general election under the Ballot, will fully
occupy the general mind. It remains only to
notice in a few words the spirit and temper in
which their views- were enunciated and
enforced by Mr. MULL and the other leading
speakers. The circumstance that so few
members of Parliament were present, may be
accounted for in several ways. It is certain
that more would have attended but for real
hindrances; and we know the way in which
gentlemen take fright at the bare idea of
"breaking up the party." As it was, there was
some difference, in degree of temper and of self-
control between the foremost man there and the
bulk of those who listened with deference to
him. We have no fear, however, that the
advocates of disestablishment will be precipi-
tated into premature action. They can dis-
tinguish very well between the education
quarrel and that great matter which, to their
minds, includes all others. It is for the
Whiggish sections of the Liberal party, and
especially for their leaders, to take a just
measure of this strong demonstration and of
what it bodes. They will not now be expected
to apply their own rule for Ireland to England
and Scotland; but they will be expected to
make the necessary amendments in the Eng-
lish Education Act, without allowing another
Session to pass away, or in spite of all the
strength that Mr. STANSFELD says they have
acquired, they will had it difficult to hold
their ground.

articles.title: LORD CARNARVON AND PAID AGENTS.
articles.text:
LORD CARNARVON AND PAID
AGENTS.

THE one cry sent up by our country gentle-
men, whether of the Parliament or only of
the " eastalorum and rotolorum," have been
telling us that all would be well with the
agricultural labourers if " agitators " bad not
got in amongst them. The belief sought to
be inculcated by those highly respectable per-
sons is that all actual and threatened mischief '
must be connected with the misrepresenta-
tions of these messengers of mischief, and not
from short wages, pinched meals, or frowzy
cottages. If this be the case, who can say
that these respectable persons have not good
cause for denouncing "paid agents," or that
friends of peace and order everywhere should
not back them up in their attempts to stamp
out a pest more dangerous than the cattle
plague.
There is an Agricultural Labourers' League
at Leamington, and this League employs
agents who travel the country more rapidly
than the rinderpest. They haunt rural bye-
lanes, insinuate themselves into the village
tavern, hitherto the seat of innocence ; crouch
behind barn doors, keeping at a distance how-
ever from the horseponds ; and sometimes,
when the fear of the squire is not before their
eyes, they harangue the simple-minded rustics
from under the shady branches of the village
; oak, and render them discontented by telling
them, what, of course, they were not in the
least aware of previously, that what they get
for their work is not enough to keep body
and soul together. And put other wicked
thoughts into their heads, assuring them by
union with each other they will be enabled to
improve their condition by getting: more
money, and therefore more and better
food and, clothing, and decenter habitations for
themselves and their children.

The candid portion of our gentry admit that
something should be done. Lord CARNAUVON
speaks out openly enough on this head, but he
objects to what is proposed on the labourers
behalf, and even strikes heavily with clenched
fist at "outside" agents who, as he declares,
have no right to interfere. We do not wish to
say a word against Lord CARNARVON, who is
one of the honestest men among the landlords
who have as yet spoken on this question.
And particularly we do not wish to mention
him with unkindness, because he did make a
practical proposal favourable to the labourers.
This of itself takes him out of the catgeorY of

9

those whose talk is meant to confuse the
public mind, and not to enlighten it, and
whose object generally seems to be to condemn
what they are incapable of reasoning against,
and to bear down by the help of prejudice
what they cannot resist by argument founded
in fact and common sense.

We have a right to ask, however, what
sense there is in the outcry against paid
agents? If the work these men are engaged
in be a legal work—if they believe it to be a
necessary and an honest work, and if others
pay them for doing it, why should the land.
lords or any body else object? This kind of
meaningless outcry was at one time got up
against men at the head of Trades Unions,
but it died out through its transparent silli-
ness, it was felt by working men that if they
required the services of others to carry on the
business necessarily connected with their
trades organizations they must pay for their
services. They bad sense enough to see that
if the Church needs agents to work its organ-
izations, such agents are paid and, as a rule,
well paid, their labour, though no doubt a
very good labour, being not sufficiently its
own reward. The army and navy have their
agents, who do not live on the smell of gun-
powder or bilge water, but on the hard cash
they receive for the performance of their
duties. The Government has its agents all
over the world, and pays them. The com-
mercial classes have their agents, who go
through the commonplace form of receiving
periodical cheques for what they do. Our
great missionary societies send agents amongst
the savages to all ends of the earth, but they
provide them with current cash that they may
pay their butchers' bills. Parliamentary

agents get their" screws" for doing the shabby
work in which they are sometimes engaged.
Who, in this world, where tradesmen's
accounts must ho paid, works for nothing?
Mr. GLADSTONE pockets his annual stipend.
Mr. DISRAELt bags his pension. Archbishops
and bishops, though self-denying as a rule, do
not refuse the filthy lucre which their gene-
rous mother, the Church, slips into their
sleeves. Why should all these be paid, and
Mr. ARCH and his fellow labourers go without?
He may not be as holy as a bishop, or as
highly placed as a Prime Minister, actual or
expectant, but he must live, und as a honest
labourer he is as worthy of his poor hire as is
either bishop or statesman. They daily solace
themselves with " potage," "Poisson," "en-
trees," " releves," and other enticing luxuries,
washed down with Marcobrunner, sparkling
champagne, old crusted port, and golden
sherry; and need not be angry if the potatoes
on his dish are multiplied, whilst he is labour-
ing with more honest thoughtfulness than
nature has given most of them the capability
of acquiring, to add to the comfort of poor
peasants' homes.
Lord CARNARVON and the others who have per-
mitted themselves to talk nonsense against the
paid agents of the Leamington Union should
make their censure more inclusive, or it will be
worth nothing. At present it does not even
look honest. It is a trick, and a very old one,
like ring dropping •or skittle sharping. If
labouring men could be brought to put aside
paid agents, the farmers and landholders
would fling their hats and coronets into the
air for very joy, just as the wolves might be
supposed to caper if the sheep refused a
mouthful to the dogs who kept watch for their
protection.
The labourers have trusted for several
hundred years to the justice and kindness of
their landlords. Let them try ten years of
work with good unions and active agents, and
they will have convinced themselves which
policy is the best. Nay the one year of
agitation, of d emand, of manliness, has done more
for them than bishops, lords, squires, farmers,
and all the rest of their natural benefactors
have accomplished on their behalf in a century.
Poor HonoE is beginning to look around hint
and see things in their right light, and is not
likely to go submissively to those benefactors,
and permit them to again "draw the wool
over his eyes."

articles.title: SOUND AN ALARM.
articles.text:
SOUND AN ALARM.

•
In a leading article on Saturday last in tha
Times the following words appeared :—it We

gather from Mr. LOWE'S address that a great
social and. economical danger threatens us
from the sudden rise and extension of unsound
doctrines. The idea, of Co-operation has taken
possession of men's minds, and developed
itself to such an extent that it may rival the
evils of Communism. Strikes, rattening,
combinations against masters, or against non-
unionist or now hands, represent the organiza-
tion of. labour as it is understood by the
workman."

This is a very alarming state of things, and
if it exists the country owes a deep debt of
gratitude to Mr. LOWE and the Times for
pointing it out. If the nation is becoming
daily worse, and passing almost unconsciously
into a deadly anarchy, it is a blessing we have
a newspaper with courage enough to speak
out and warn us of the gulf towards which
we are so rapidly moving. The question in
the first place to be settled, Uowever, is one of
fact, Is it so? That Co-operation has taken
possession of men's minds and is rapidly
developing itself, is certainly true; but we do
not see very clearly in what way it is to rival
the "evils of Communism." What these evils
are has not been stated. The writer of the
article has adopted the wiser course of leaving
the reader to guess. The word " Cominunism "
may simply have reference to the Commune as
was the case recently in Paris. It may mean
common duties in work, and common property
in goods and chattels; or it may mean murder,
or arson, or burglary, or area-sneaking. As
the Times applies it the French form cannot
be meant, as English Co-operators do not
meddle with matters of Government, local or
general. It can hardly mean community of
goods, inasmuch as in their stores and factories
the minutest attention is paid by co-operators
to individual right, and the utmost strictness
observed in apportioning to each individual
h 4 fair, share of the joint property. It
cannot be murder, as no case has as yet been
brought 'under the notice of the authorities.
Even Mr. Low; though he journeyed amongst
thousands of co-operators, escaped scot free,
Arson is out of the question, as the co-epera7
tors are great builders of property; they have
invested many hundreds of thousands of
pounds in the erection of houses, stores, and
factories, but have not brought themselves
under the notice of the public by burning
anything except coal and gas honestly bought
and paid for. Were it burglary, they would
have .to break into each other's houses, and by
the time the game had gone round, the dividend
on the profit resulting from it would be small.
Area-sneaking would not do; honest work pays
better.

We have exhausted our gussets. What, we
ask therefore, eau the Times mean? We
wait for a reply, and pass on to our Trades
Union friends, who it scorns possess certain
queer notions on the subject of "organization
qf labour," With them it does not mean
wing their own capital for self-employment;
it does not mean oven a common understanding
for their mutual advantage, such as the Unions
of the engineers, ironfounders, and other
existing bodies. The _Tittles knows all about
it however. It has lifted up a corner of the
curtain bel4cd which the devilish plans of
England's working men arc laid, and gives an
alarming description of the dreadful proceed-
ings carried on—if Strikes," " rattoning,"
"combinations against masters, or against
non-unionist, or new hands." The result of
this, no doubt, is dreadful if we could see
it, Working men, by their strikes, taking all
the profit of the nation's industry, and leaving
nothing to capital; ovary man stealing every
other man's tools, so as to prevent any work
from being done; every employer combined
against; every non-unionist going in fear of
his life ; every " new hand" driven out ;
nobody at work but a few selfish, jealous,
grey -headed oia trades unionists, who have
taken possession of the workshops of England,
and stand triumphant in the midst of the
industrial ruin they have brought upon the
country.

If ws gather this from Mr. Lowies speech,
and from the Times article on it, there ii more
profit than pleasure derived from a study of
the picture presented to us, We hope it is over-
coloured, as wOll as Oxaggertged in the drawing.
Mr. J/JWE 18 not alyiaTs to 49 134104 on and

the Times is not absolutely infallible. It
has been known to get away from the strict
truth upon one or two occasions. Let us hope
that such is the case in the present instance.
LEO;II Luvr's new book, "The History of
British Commerce and the Economic Progress
of the British Nation from 1763 to 1870,"
gives us ground for this hope. He informs us
that in 18-13 the total value of property and
profits assessed to income tax, was two
hundred and fifty-one millions sterling ;
whilst in 1870 it amounted to four hundred
and nine millions sterling. We do not
say that this disproves the statement of
the Times, inasmuch as the odd hundred and
fifty-eight millions may have been forgotten or
overlooked by our communist co-operators
and rattening trades unionists, in their hurry
to run away with everything else. That there
is some truth in the statements of the Times
may be proved by this other fact stated by
Professor LEmsa LEVI; in 1830 the depositors
in savings banks were only 412,217 persons,
and their deposits amounted to only 13 millions
and a half. In 1870, the depositors had
increased to 2,568,000 persons, and the money
deposited to £53,000,000. The difference is
no doubt made up of money stolen by the
working people from the propertied classes.
How else could it have got into their hands?
Some stop ought to be put to such dangerous
proceedings, or the very worst consequences
may be looked for. We have got the Times
and Mr. LOWE however, who with their love
of truth and their higher economic teaching
will some day put us right, especially if the
working people will only listen to them, and
believe them. We are compelled to say, how-
ever, that at present there does not appear to
be much reason to expect that such will be the
case, and, therefore, perhaps, on the whole, the
best thing we can do is to shut our eyes, and
go to old scratch without making too much of
a row about the matter.

articles.title: INTIMIDATION.
articles.text:
INTIMIDATION.

A JOURNEYMAN baker named GEORGE
SuErFtimn has been sent to the House of
Correction for seven days, with bard labour,
for obstructing a fellow-workman named
SANDERS who wished to return to his employ-
ment on the old conditions and, as a matter of
course, in opposition to the wishes of the
Union. GEORGE SHEFFIELD does not of him-
self seem to have done much to call for so
heavy a punishment; but it was sufficiently
clear that he had acted in connection with
others who did break the law, by Reeking to
prevent a man from going to work who desired
to do so.

We give no opinion on the character of the
punishment, but we consider it our ditty to
inform working men on strike that they inflict
' serious injury on the cause of Trades
Unionism when in any way they break the
law, or seek unduly to prevent any member of
a trade from acting as seems right in his own
oyes. The best men in Trade Societies strongly
disapprove of such action. They know that
the strength of Union is in the righteous-
ness of its aims; and they know also that
when the objects sought by bodies of men are
legitimate and proper, peace and reason are
the best agents that can be employed for their
promotion, We arc perfectly aware that the
tempers of Union men are frequently very
much tried by the conduct of weak brethren,
who, at a critical moment, betray their cause by
throwing down their arms and surrendering to
tho employers ; but it is their highest duty
under such circumstances to conquer their
tempers', abstain from anything that can be
construed, into violence,- and win their fight '
by always keeping the law on their side. Too
much stress cannOt be laid on this, and there-
fore we. urge it with great earnestness, and
trust that in all trades on strike every man
who can exercise any influence will do so on
the side of legality and peace. Working men
may really make themselves masters of the
satiation by keeping law and reason always in
view, and by thus gaining, as they inevitably
must, the good will and support of all disin-
terested honest MM.

OUR DEBT TO AIIEitICA.
SINCE he reasons gOien by the Geneva
4bitratore for the dooisie4 equie 0 have beep

published, there has been more than enough
of newspaper discussion on the subject. There
existed, it appears, amongst the persons assem-
bled much divergence of view—as to inter-
national law in its letter and essence, as to
the new rules by which the facts adduced
were to be judged, and in accordance with
which the award was to be given. Sir Aux.

COCKBURN, there cannot be the least doubt, is
an able lawyer, who understood the case in its
legal aspect, and who argued it with great
force, and our newspapers, in following him,
cannot fail to stand on tolerably arm ground.
But when everything has been said that can
be said as to international law and duty, the deci-
sion in reference to any act brought in question
must nearly altogether rest on the spirit, more or
less evident, by which such act was prompted.
And this, we take it, will govern all future
decisions on international questions referred to
arbitration. It is all very well to pooh-pooh
the sentimental side of such questions, and to
declare that Governments have nothing to do
with them; but if those who do so will
examine this Alabama question, they will see
that a good deal of what we have to pay, if
not every penny of it, belongs to the senti-
mental side only.
That the leading statesmen of England, the
Parliament of England, the press of England,
and .what may be called the middle and upper
classes
,of England were unfriendly to the
Government of America during the civil war
is as certain as any known and generally ad-
mitted historical fact. The escape of the
Alabama was winked at, its exploits were ap-
proved of, its destruction was deplored. In a
dry legal argument much might be said and
proved as to the escape of this vessel, which
would have removed blame from our Govern-
ment and its officials at home and abroad.
And if the spirit of the nation had been as
friendly towards America as it was evidently
unfriendly, the three millions never would
have been scored up against us. The spirit dis-
played in England by the persons referred to
explains the character of the act, and in the
light thrown on it by our undisguised rejoic-
ings, and in a consideration the gain our
merchants and others made of it, there could
be no mistake why the thing took place, nor
can there be much doubt as to the justice of
the decision which places on us the necessity
of making some sort of reparation for the
damage done.

Our conduct as a people—always except-
ing the working men of England, who
from first to last, noted in a noble allegiance
to principle and duty.-was utterly disgrace-
ful. We cannot, we must not, forget the
baseness of or leading journals. The Times,
the Standard, and the Tekyrap4 vied with
each other in vileness of spirit, in exuberance
of malignancy; in a mendacity which had
neither limit nor forbearance. We have to
pay now for the culpable immobility of Earl
RussEu, ; for the unpatriotic selfishness of the
Limns and their supporters, and for the dis-
honesty of local officials. But we have also to
pay for the unprincipled, dishonest, and in-
salting diatribes of our newspaper press,
which, notwithstanding the mischief it has
already done, whines and grumbles still in the

THE WORIMEN'S PEACE ASSOCIATION.
The Council of the Workmen's Pease Associa-
tion, being unable to send representatives to the
Congress of Peace and Liberty, held at Lugano,
in Switzerland, but desirous that their opiuions
should be known to the Congress, adopted the
following resolutions, which were forwarded to the
secretary of the Congress, with the request that
they be read to the delegates assembled :—" That
this Council, though unable to send a delegation
to the annual congress of the League of Peace
and Liberty at Lugano, desires to express its
sympathy with all earnest friends of peace on the
Continent. The
.council ,observes with pleasure
that the history of international arbitration, and
the best means of making it applicable, are set
down among the princilial subjects of discnssion at
the Congress. At the same time it would express
the earnest hope that the members of the Con-
gress will declare. once more against the war
theory, inasmuch as the industrial classes, no
matter what the nature of the war, are always
the greatest sufferer." "That as an earnest effort
will be made in the next session of the British
Parliament to induce the British Government to
take the initiative in passing a code of international
law and the establishment of an international
tribunal to administer such law, this council in-
vites all friends of peace to initiate and heartily
support similar efforts in their respective countries,
as we believe such means to be at once the nest
efficacious in preventing war, and be most prac-
tical in rendering useless fighting forces."

articles.title: DEMONSTRATION OF RAILWAY
articles.text:
DEMONSTRATION OF RAILWAY

SERVANTS.

On Sunday afternoon a demonstration of rail-
way employs of all grades took place in Hyde
Park, under the auspices of a committee formed
of several of the leading members of the Amal-
gamated Society of Railway Servants. The
immediate object of the meeting was the support
of the emigration movement now in progress
amongst railway servants, especially in connection
with those who lost their situations through the
late strike on the Loudon and North-Western
Railway.

According to previous arrangements, shortly
after two o'clock, the men belonging to the diffe-
rent railways assembled in Trafalgar-square, those
from the London and North-Western and the
London and South-Western coming up in pro-
cession, each accompanied by their own band. A
considerable number of the men wore their uni-
forms, ana amongst them were guards, ticket
collectors, policemen, porters, &c. At a few
minutes before 3 o'clock about 3,000 rnen were
assembled. They were marshalled in procession,
preceded by the Royal standard, and a flag on
which was inscribed "Union is strength," and,
accompanied by the bands, marched four abreast
through Pall-mall, St. James's•street, and Picca-
dilly, to Hyde Park. Just as the procession
entered the park a heavy storm of rain came on,
' but the rain did not appear to damp the ardour of
the processionists, who kept on their way to the
place appointed by the meeting, near the " Re-
formers"rree." They were joined by a large
body of the men from the Great Western Railway
and other lines, bringing the total number of those
present up to about 6,000 persons, nearly all of
whom appeared to be connected with railways.

The proceedings were at once commeneed by
Dr. Baxter Langley being moved to the chair.
Having explained the object of the meeting, he
entered at some length into the position of railway
servants generally, and the efforts that were
being made to ameliorate their condition, which
in many instances was that of slavery.
The meeting was then addressed by Messrs.
Sampson, Hayward, Elliott, Fisk, Shrines, Bowles,
Chapman, and other railway emplo3 is, on the
advantages that would accrue from emigration on
a large scale, and illustrating the bad treatment
the men receive from many of the railway coru-
/mules. The following resolution was carried by
acclamation :

That this meeting thoroughly approves of the
action of the Amalgamated Society of Railway
Servants in raising funds to assist all classes of
railway employtis wishing to emigrate to wider
fields of industry, where labour r. ceives its just
reward, and is not subject to the ruling of such
tyrannical despotisms as was recently witnessed
in connection with the London and North-Western
Railway Company. And this meeting hereby
pledges itself to use all legal efforts in promoting
the same, and further protests against the lino of
policy adopted by the London and North-Westera
Railway directors in refusing to submit the ques-
tion lately in dispute between them and their em-
ploye's to arbitration, and strongly condemns the
language used by Mr. Cawkwell in stating that
the matters in dispute did not admit of discussion.
A vote of thanks was thou given to the chair-
man, and the meeting was concluded. The pro-
cession was then re-formeil, and returned by the
same route to T rafalgar-square, and then dis-
persed.

GREAT FIRE IN THAMES-STREET.

BISHOP ELLICOTT AND THE AGRI-
CULTURAL LABOURERS.

On Saturday a conference of an unusual
character was hold at the Bishop's Palace,
Gloucester, between eight agricultural labour-
ers, with the district secretary of the Agri-
cultinal Union, Mr. Yeates, and the Bishop of
Gloucester and Bristol, to consider the best
means of improving the condition of the
agricultural labourer. Mr. Price, M.P., chair-
man of the Midland Railway Company, and
several leading agriculturists took part in the
conference, which lasted seven hours.
The Bishop said it must be understood that
it was not a conference between employers
and employed, as he had no right to call such
a meeting, besides which one of the parties
most concerned—the tenant farmers—were
not represented. He simply wished it to be a
friendly meeting between himself and some
of the labourers in the diocese, so that while
keeping within his indisputable province as
Bishop he might hear any complaints they
had to make of any grievances or hardshipsunder
which they were now labouring, or any which
they anticipated. He believed that faithful and
sober people who had considered the subject
agreed that there were four ways in which the
condition of the agricultural labourer might be
greatly advanced and benefited. These were
—better education, better home aecommoda-
tion, an increased interest in the land which
, the labourer assisted in cultivating, and an
improvement in his wages. No thoughtful
man meant that education should be confined,
to the more teaching the labourer to read and
write, but that he should be taught self-respect
—be made more and more to consider himself
and the position which he occupied, and be led
on more and to see that he had a defined
position by God in which he should humbly
endeavour to do his duty. That-the labourer
should be better housed, he thought would be
as readily admitted as that he should be bettor
educated; and he was glad to see every-
where inolications that the landlords were
desirous of making an improvement in this re-
spect. The effect of this would be to raise the
moral tone of the labourer, inasmuch as im-
proved house accommodation would lead him
to improve himself; but he hoped the milli
beneficent efforts of the landlords in this respect
would not be frustrated by the labourers taking
in lodgers, and so making things as -bad as
they wore before. The third method sug-
gested of improving the labourer's (condition—
that of giving him a direct interest in the land
—was a most difficult question to deal with.
What he (the Bishop) was in favour of was
that the deserving labourer should have
assigned to him a certain portion of ground,
say from three roods to half an acre, so that
he might exercise that love of fluctuation and
chance which seemed to attend agricultural
preparation and its results. He thought all
would argreo that the labourer ought to re-
ceive more wages. It would be imprudent
for him to express any opinion as to what
that improvement should be • but he might
venture to say that there would be an increase
in the weekly wage, and that the system of
giving beer and cider might be abolished in
favour of an vittivalent Pll3ll payment. News-
papers told us that what had been called the
feudal system, or what -little remained of it,
was fast passing away. Commercial laws
were rapidly becoming applied to agricultural
pursuits ; and those great principles which
governed trade were now being
applied to the
cultivation of the land. And there was no
disguising the fact that those changes would
inflict suffering upon all parties eoncerned,
though he might venture to say the labourers
would have to bear the least portion of the.
burden. But he might also say that those
trials would be greatly mitigated if all would
resolve to consider one another's interest, and
act up to the golden rule which the Great
Master gave in his sermon on the mount, to
do to others as they would have otheis do to
them.

The eight labourers itocompanying Mr. •
Yeates were then questioned at some length
by the Bishop and his friends as to th„eir
position and earnings, and the grievoms
under which they laboured. This ooeuplect

some time. It appeared that the wages of the
men averaged about 10s. or lls, per week for
working 14 to 16 hours per day; some of

majority of cases, according to the men's story,
little better than miserable hovels. Most of

The higher wages obtained by labourers at

rence calls upon those who have at heart the

- -

Mr. Herbert New, of Eversham, supported

mously.
Mr. E. Wall, M.P. (who was received with

The Rev. J. T. Brown read a paper on "The

The Rev, IL W. Crossicey moved the follow-

That this Conference recommends the society's

of disestablishment; third, to the improvement
and extension of their organization in every dis-
trict; and especially, fourth, to such wise and

will enable them to exert utmost strength in the

Mr. E. Ashworth seconded the resolution,.

The evening meeting was held in the Town

lain; and upon the platform were Mr. Miall,

worth, M.P., in addition to most of the

bered about 2,500, and they enthusiastically
applauded the salient points in the speeches.
Mr. Illingworth, M.P., moved :

That this meeting highly approve of the motion
in favour of the disestablishment of the English
and Scottish Claurehes, of whieh Mr. Miall, M.P.,
has given notice for.neit session, caul that it desires

Mr. E. A. Leatham, M.P., seconded the
motion.
The resolution was carried.
Mr. R. W. Dales, of Birmingham, next
moved— _ _ _

That, in accordance with the resolution almady
adopted, the meeting resolves that the following
petition be presented to the House of Commons,
and authorizes the chairman to sign the same on
its behalf:—

"To the Honourable the Commons of Great
Britain and Ireland in Parliament as3enibled.

"The humble petition of certain inhabitants of
Birmingham in public meeting assembled showeth :
That your petitioners are of opinion that all classes
of her Majesty's subjects should, in regard to the
action of the State in respect to religion, be placed
on is footing of perfect equality. That while,
by moans of modern legislation, much progress has
been made towards the possession of such equality,
it cannot be fully enjoyed while two religious
bodies are established by law and supported by

of the community. That the Established Churches
are admitted to stand in need of extensive re-
forms, not only to put an end to serious scandals,

as religious institutions. That it is useless to
attempt to effect such reforms so long us the

ment, which, from its composition, is incompetent

of reformation must devolve on the members of
the Established Churches; but for that purpose

for religion and beneficial to the whole com-
munity. They therefore pray your Honourable
House to adopt measures by which disestablish-
ment and disendownient may be effected; and
your petitioners will ever pray."
The Rev. J. S. Withington, President of the

resolution' *hioh, with the petition, was

THE LABOUR REPRESENTATION
LEAGUE AND THE BALLOT TRICK.

At a meeting of the Labour Representation
League, lately held at Cockspur-street,
Charing-cross, Mr. R. M. Latham, the Presi-
dent, in opening the business of the evening,
remarked that with regard to the action of the
Conservative party in their efforts to defeat
the intention of the Ballot Act at the recent
election at Preston, the officers of the League
had during the present week been in com-
munication with the working-men and Liberal
electors of Preston in order to ascertain precise
partieulars as to the working of the machinery
which was then put in motion. The following
letter, he stated, had been received that
morning from Mr. A. W. Bailey, the Liberal
Agent for Preston and President of the
Amalgamated Society of Tailors of Great
Britain:

175, North•road, Preaton, Sept. 26, 1872.
Dear Sir,—Your letter is to hand. The way
the card trick was worked was as follows :—The
night before they (the Conservatives) sent the
tickets to all the voters that had promised their
votes, telling them to give their tickets to the man
at the door. Two men stood at tho door with
large papers on their hats—blue, of course. The
voters, I expect, thought they ware going to get
something for their tickets. Every voter who
came out was asket by those men for his ticket,
and if he did not deliver one up the Conservatives
put him down as being against them. They were
thus able to calculate within nine at the end. I
don't think that any one should be allowed to
stand at the doors, for in many cases they could
see into the room. I enclose two of the tickets.
Hoping you will he the means of putting a stop
to such unfair work on any side, I remain yours
truly,
- ALFRED W. BAILEY.
To Mr. Thomas Mottershead, Secretary of the
Labour Representation League.
The Preston card trick was, he thought, a
striking illustration of the dishonest shifts men
would resort to for the purpose of preserving
their coercive power over the action of poor
and dependent men, and it was the duty of the
members of the League' in common with all
honest men, to use their best exertions in
putting an end to such a discreditable violation
of the evident intent of the Ballot Ad. Of
the numerous evils which the intimidation,
lavish expenditure of money, and general
corruption sanctioned under the old system of
Parliamentary eleotion had given birth to, none
was more destruetive of freedom of election
than the.employment of paid agents, an un-
scrupulous body of men, whose actions tended
only, and Still tends, to unfairly augment the
power of the puree, and-keep alive nefarious
practices such as the one the League had then
met to consider. It appeared to him that two
things were required, namely, to call upon the
Legislature---lst. To abolish paid agents by
Ast of Parliament. 2nd. To pass a Bill dealer-
ing that the intention of the Ballot Act was to
provide for the independent and untrammelled
exercise of the franchise by means of secret
voting, and that any violation or evasion of
that intention either by the collection of cards
after polling, prying into the balloting
chambers, or otherwise, should be punishable
as a misdemeanour. He also advised that a
memorial embodying the whole facts of the
proceedings at the Preston election, and suggest-
ing these or other sufficient remedies' should
be drawn up and presented. to the Govern.
mat,

A discussion'ensued, in which Messrs. Allan,
Broadhurst, Sinclair, Baker, Eccarius, and
Mottershead, took part; and a resolution was
carried, on the motion of Mr. William Allan,
to the effect that a memorial to the Govern-
ment be drawn up embodying the hots
conneeted with the Preston election, and calling
upon the Legislature to amend the Ballot Act
in such a way as would prevent the recurrence
at future elections of the improper practices
omplained of.

articles.text:
THE METROPOLITAN POLICE AND
THEIR PAY.

The following is the reply of Colonel Hender-
son, the Chief Commissioner of the Metropoli-
tan Police, to ,a letter that had been sent by
the police, asking for an advance of wages,
owing to the increase in the price of provisions,
and the high rate paid for lodging accammoaa-
tion :—" I have carefully considered the
petition of the sergeants and constables of the
N Division, and with every wish to do all in
my power for the welfare and comfort of the
metropolitan police, I repeat that I do not at
present feel justified in recommending to the
Secretary of State for the Home Department an
increase of their pay. It is only very recently
that the pay and emoluments of the force have
been augmented, and in the present state of
the 'police funds' an application to Parliament
for an increased vote would be necessary be-
fore any further increase would be granted,
and I am unable
.to see , sufficient grounds to
justify such an application," All the men are
very much dissatisfied with this decision, and
though all classes get an increase of about is.
per week, the men liave had two days leave
stopped in a month.

CORRESPONDENCE.

MINERS AND TIIEIR DWELLINGS.
To the Editor of the BEE

Sin,—Will you allow me space to call atten-
tion to the above question, believing that it
underlies in a great measure the future pro-
gress of the miners as a class It is a very
great grievance, and one we are utterly power-
less to remedy without very great changes
are brought about by the overpowering pres-
sure of public opinion, as by the present
system the employer finds the houses. The
cottage 'I occupy, and it is a sample of too
many, consists ot a single room on the ground
floor—fourteen feet by eleven feet by seven
feet high—an attic over it reached by a ladder
(by-the-bye, a poor woman was killed by fall-
ing down one last week). The attic is the
same size as the house, with this exception it
is only three feet six inches high at the sides,
and rises to nine feet in the centre; being
roofed with red pantiles, in bad repair, it
admits wind and water plentifully. I have
also a small pantry built to the house in an
afterthought. Now in this miserable hole
myself, wife' and five children have to exist;
we must either all sleep in the downstairs
room, where all our washing, cooking, &e.,
has been done, or I must send my, bairns to
sleep •in the before-mentioned attic, which,
from being roofed with pantiles is like a
baker's oven in summer time, and as cold as
the snow hut of the Esquimaux.
This is not the worst, as, although there
are not less than two hundred and fifty
cottages at Seghill where I now am, there is
not one single provision made for sanitary
purposes, neither water-closet nor midden-
stead ; and I am sure that I should scarcely
be believed were I to attempt to describe the
scenes one has to witness.

A short time ago the Northumberland
Miners' Mutual Confident Association took
the matter up, and in an interview with the
Steam Coal Owners' Association, brought the
matter under their notice with the hope that
something would be 'done to bring about a
better state of things; they (the owners)
argued that as a society they could not take
it un ; but recommended the men to take local
action at their own collieries, and promised to
use whatever influence they had to help us,
who were worst. At our firsb interview' our
employer, J. Layeock, Esq., promised to do
something, but did not start. We saw him
again last week, when he told us, in a very
curt manner, almost amounting to (dare I say
it) impertinence, that he should do what he
liked when he liked, and those who did not
like the houses could leave them, a speech
that he had a perfect right to utter in these
times; but he would be the first to cry. out
about the tyranny of the working man if we
were to take him at. his word.

But, Mr. Editor, there is a point in a ques-
tion like this a long way above the common
ideas of abstract right. We are not made into
skilled pitmen all at (Mee, and when we have
reached this, anything that takes away our
capacity for work is an injury to society; and
besidag they are continually crying out about
our debased habits. What can they expect
under the circumstances here described? .
Without a great alteration in our domestic
aocommedation, we shall get worse instead of
better, as our daughters are tho mothers of
the generation that syet to come; and it is for
the present. to decide in a great measure what
the future shall be.-" Yours, -
JOUN Smrur, Pitman.

LATEST INTELLIGENCE.

FRIDAY.

We regret to announce that the Right Hon.
Sir James S. Willes, a justice of the Contmon
Pleas has committed suicide. It.seems that
Mr. justice Wiles, who suffered a good deal
from gout, had recently returned to Otterspool,
near Watford, having been on circuit. The
day before yesterday he was twice out rowing
on the Colne, which run through his garden ;
but yesterday morning, about half-past seven
o'clock, he shot himself. The gout had, it ie
believed, become suddenly suppressed, and the
malady, as frequently happens, had affected
the brain.

Mr. Registrar Spring Rice had before him
at the Court of Bankruptcy, yesterdap the
matter of Thomas Pox Crop. The ebtor,
who carried on business at 2, Devonshire-
square, City, as a silk packer and shipping ana

Clapham Rise, breeder of racehorses, has pre-
sented a petition of liquidation, estimating

£6OO. Upon the application of M. J. ".
Watson, of Basinghall-street, solicitor, his
Honour appointed Mr. F. Cates, public ac-
countant of King William-street, receiver,
and granted an interim injunction restraining
the action at law of a suing debtor.
A Melbourne telegram says that new gold-
fields have been discovered at Yam Creek, 150
miles from Port Darwin. Several hundred
miners have gone there.

Father Hyacinthe . has just applied to the -
Frerleh tribunals for the validation of his civil
marriage.

New Conservative Club has been opened
this week at Sunderland. According to the
Newcastle Journal, it commences with every
indication of becoming a complete success, and
doubtless will be fully appreciated and sup-
ported by the Conservatives of Sunderland.
At a meeting of the Belfast Town Council
on Tuesday, a letter was read from the Under
Secretary to the effect that a memorial front
the Council for a commission to inquire into
the late riots would be laid before the Lords
Justices.

The horses bought by the Government for
the Autumn Manceuvres are now being sold
off at good prices. They were bought at £3B
a head, and they are now selling at about £35.
The returns of the number and tonnage of
the vessels launched in the Clyde during the
month and three months just closed show a
considerable increase, compared with the
corresponding periods of the four preceding
years.

The inquest on Sarah Hurwin Rymer, who
died from a kick on the chest given to her by
her son, John Thomas Rymer, has resulted in
a verdict of manslaughter, and he has been
committed to take his trial.

The Arobbishop of Canterbury continued
his visitation at the Cathedral yesterday. DI
a long charge he vindicated the principle of
the Church Establishment, showing that lho
poor would be neglected by congregational
bodies and contending that the Establishment
possessed great advantages over voluntary
bodies endowed. Dissenting bodies were
amenable to civil courts, and their doctrinee
had been declined in those courts.

those of the Chancellor of the Exchequer ill

observed that the right of the Crown to hunt

THE WEEK'S NEWS.

On Monday Sir Charles Dilke delivered an
address in the City Hall, of Glasgow, on Class
Legislation.

Some peculiar claims have been allowed by
the Revising Barrister in Finsbury. Joint
occupancy, as by partners, was held to entitle
each partner to a vote where the rental ex-
ceeded double the statutable qualification.
Or. Fergussou was put on the roll in respect
of his stable.

M. Gambetta is still carrying the Red Cross
through the rural departments. At Evian
and Thonon he was visited by a number of
French and Swiss deputations apparently
Wanting more orations from him. His organ,
the .Republique Franquise, has fallen out with
that of the President about the moral effect
of his starring tour. It is maintained by the
former "to be profitable to the Republic."

John Metcalfe, of the Waterloo Arms in
Marylebone, has received a warning on the
subject of harbouring criminals. Au inspector
found in his parlour one night several con-
victed thieves, and informed the landlord of
their presence. He turned them all out of
the room, but on .returning the inspector saw
half a dozen of them still in the bar. The
information was dismissed with a caution.

In Clerkenwell the publicans are being
zealously supported by the magistrates in
their endeavours to keep orderly houses. Two
men charged with creating disturbances on
being refused beer because they were intoxi-
cated, were lined respectively 208 and 255.
Nevertheless, among the "night charges" at
the same court, there were as many as 36 for
drunkenness.

Sir W. Bodkin had a lengthy calendnr at
the adjourned Middlesex Sessions. It com-
prised 97 committals, of which 83 were for
felony, and the rest for misdemeanour.

General Faidberbe has had another inter-
view with the President. On Sunday the
Earl and Countess of Stanhope dined with M.
Thiers.

Republican Algiers covets the honour of
being represented in the National Assembly by
Victor Hugo.

By the Bill which has been submitted to
the Spanish Cortes for transferring the pay-
ment of clerical subsidies to the municipal
authorities the Government hope to save fully
twenty -s even million pesetas.

Mr. Greeley has travelled three thousand
miles and delivered two hundred speeches in
Pennsylvania, Ohio, and Indiana. He returns
confident of the result they will produce.

An enormous quantity of jute is reported to
have been sacrificed in the late cyclone at
Calcutta. One account estimates the quantity
at 50,000 bales.

On Monday in Dean Forest, a brutal case of
sheep massacre was discovered. A miner found
seven valuable sheep with their heads beaten
to pieces, and seven others are missing. This
shocking act is believed to have been done out
of revenge, and it is attributed to a recent
prosecution conducted by the owner.

William Clarkson, a clerk, living at Selby,
Yorkshire, was on Monday fined by the local
bench at Goole 116, and £3 costs, for six
offences under the Vacoinatitm Act, viz., re-
fusing to have his three children vaccinated,
and refusing to produce them before the
magistrates. It was stated that he had been
repeatedly fined, and that his goods had been
distrained upon for similar offences. There
were now left no goods to distrain upon, and
in default of payment by any means Clarkson
was sentenced to terms of imprisonment
amounting to three months.

An account of the election expenses incurred
at Pontefract (the first under the ballot) of
both candidates has been published, and it
gives absolute proof of that which was sufil-
cently obvious, at least in this particular case
—that the cost of candidature is largely reduced
under the new system. " The total charge
incurred on behalf of Mr. Childers is stated to
be £243 16s. Bcl., and that of Lord PoHinton
as £426 Os, 6d„

The latest accounts from Irelard of the
harvest are much more re-assuring, especially
from the North; but the potato crop, though
in some parts better than expected, is in many
districts a complete failure.

Mr, Forbes, the managing director of the
London, Chatham, and Dover Railway Com-
pany, has increased the salaries of his clerks,
some RIO and others Lb S per annum, accord-
ing to merit and seniority. The great increase
of traffic on the railway has also induced
Mr. Forbes to raise tile notaries of number
of statiolarromtsrh

Something like an incipient strike has been
provoked among the Poor-law medical officers
by the Public Health Act. In a series of
resolutions which they passed at a meeting of
their association, it was affirmed that the
salaries are arbitrarily, fixed without regard
to any uniform standard of remuneration;
that in most instances they are inadequate;
and that the 'new duties imposed by the Act
will be impracticable if dispensaries are not
established to relieve the medical officers from
the expense of supplying medicines.

Before the Lord Mayor-eleet the British
Australian Telegraph Company has been
charged with seven days' default in not for-
warding to the Registrar a list of its share-
holders within the prescribed time after its
last general meeting. The defence that only
one day's default, had been committed, and
that the list could not be prepared earlier, was
sustained, and the information dismissed.

Early on Tuesday morning an attempt was
made at the terminus of the Cork and Bandon
Railway to steal three stand of arms on their
way to Kinsale Barracks. Timely discovery
was made, and the martial burglars fled. .

Out of the Dudley-street mystery a case of
slander has arisen, Jane Ross, who lived in
the same street, publicly accused James
Merriman, an auctioneer's porter, of having
murdered the woman found under the stairs.
He laid an information against her at Marl-
borough-street, when she was bound over to
keep the peace.

Frederick Wilson has experienced the
weight of. the new licensing law, in having
had to pay Ns. fine and costs for disorderly
behaviour in the Grapes Tavern, Bow-street.

A cabman has been fined £3 and costs for
permitting another man to use his badge and
licence. The cab-owner who employed the
latter incurred the mitigated fine of 20s. as
he pleaded ignorance of the transaction.

Sarah Grant, the servant girl at Hammer-
smith who disposed of her child by throwing
it into the Regent's Canal, has been com-
mitted for. trial.

Joseph Putnam took his sister.in-law to
the Victoria Theatre, and afterwards wished
her to go home with him instead of return-,
ing to her husband. When she refused he
threw her down and kicked her brutally, so
that she had. to be taken to the hospital.
Putnam was remanded.

Newcastle cabmen have struck against
badges. Several defaulters having been. sum-
moned, a vigorous reprisal was executed by
withdrawing all cabs from the stands.

Charles Fletoher, a beershop-keeper in St.
Martin's-lane, was fined £lO on Wednesday
for selling beer at the Star running grounds,
Fulham, without a special license.

Mr. Edmond Edmonds, a surgeon, who lived.
at Hercules-buildings, Lambeth, has com-
mitted suicide by poisoning himself with
prussio acid. Ile was seventy-six years of
ago. The coroner's jury on Wednesday
found that he suffered from mental derange-
ment.

The Metropolitan District Committees
.of
the Charity. Organisation Society dealt with
700 cases (exclusive of 503 non-resident
applicants) during the four weeks ending
September 28, 1812; 226 were dismissed, 193
were referred to legal and charitable agencies,
and 276 were assisted by grants, loans, employ-
ment, ite.

The Committee of the Deaf and Dumb
Asylum, Old Kent-roan, acknowledge a dona-
tion of Xl,OOO from "It. AL It."

According to the custom of several centuries,
Nottingham goose fair was "proclaimed"
yesterday by the mayor of that town. Of
course general holiday was kept, and the usuat
attractions of the fair were this year increased
by a dog show.

There are now upon the roll of the London
United District Widows' and Orphans' Fund
in connection with the Order of Foresters
some 1,200 widows and nearly as many child-
ren. The Forester states that some cases of
imposition of a very gross description have
recently come to light, and advises the board
to remember the advice which Mr. Weller
gave to his son.

At Wincanton on Wednesday, Charles Par-
sons, labourer, was committed for trial by the
county bench on the charge of wilful negli-
gence, in driving cattle across the Somerset
and Dorset Railway, at South Cheriton,
whereby three were killed by a goods train.
Mr. William Wadharn stated be censured
Parsons for driving the beasts across, and told
him that there ought to have been two men,
and that ho should not have opened the gates
before the cattle WITO got together•

On Saturday night a sad occurrence took
place at the South Pier, Sunderland. A
married woman, named Potts, who was in-
tending to proceed to London by the Have-
lock steamer, in order to reside with some
friends, her husband having deserted her, was
taking a stroll upon the pier with her two
children, when the latter, who had strayed
some Ilistance from her, were blown into the
water by a sudien gust of wind. In response
to Mrs. Potts's cries for assistance, some
Custom officers rowed to the spot, but could
find no trace of the children. One of the bodies
was subsequently recovered.

The Government of the Sultan has conceded
to the Government of Egypt perfect freedom
in the administration of all home affairs, and
in addition the right to enter into contracts for
loans to Egypt, without the previous sanction
of the Sultan.

The ship Nazarene, which left Liverpool for
Havannah on the 2.2nd of September, was lost
on Saiurday night, with all hands, at the
entrance to the Mersey. She must have
encountered the full force of the late heavy
weather in the Atlantic, and it is believed that
she had become disabled and was puffin°. back
to Liverpool for repairs when the disaster oe-
curred. The body of the master. named
Brewer, has been washed ashore. The crew
numbered seventeen men.

A farmer named Hart has been arrested for
stabbing another farmer named Reilly, near
Longford in a dispute about rent. ReilV's
injuries are terrible, the bowels protruding
through a wound in the abdomen. Little hope
is entertained of his recovery.

A meeting of the United Kingdom Alliance
held at Kidderminster en Wednesday evening
was interrupted by an opposite force. The
room was for a time a Babel of sounds, the
arguments from the platform being met with
shouting, stat-npinr, and singing. •A resolu-
tion calling for further legislative action was
passed; but a second, urging action on the
part of the electors, was declared by the
Mayor to be lost.

The Daily News states that the infirmity
of eye-sight which has led to Lord Hatherly's
resignation is due, not to any painful attack,
but to cataract, which is taking its ordinary
course. Although Lord Hatherley's resigna-
tion has been accepted, and the Queen has ex-
pressed her approval of the appointment of Sir
Roundell Palmer, that appointment can not
take place until her Majesty's next Council:

The Viking (schooner yacht) the property
of the Duke of Edinburgh, was sold by
nuntionon Wednesday at Lloyd's, and realised
£1,560,

Thomas Keel)le, a coal porter, was fined
40s. at the Greenwich Police-court on Wed-
nEsday, for using insulting language towards
the foreman of a coal wharf, who had refused
to employ unionists.

A young mannamei Robert Clarke has died
at Whitwell, Herts, from eating pickled sal-
mon, supposed to have been poisoned.

Lord 'latherley's resignation of the office o,
Lord Chancellor has been accepted. lie wit
be succeeded by Sir Roundell Palmer.

Touchingly sad has .been the death of a
French lady of rank whose exertions in the
ambulance service during the war, and the
consequent, excitement, undermined her
health. Since then the Countess de Pros has
lived at a family hotel in St. James's-place,
with her son. 'While he was on a visit to Paris

divisions of the county of Dorset, made up to
Saturday night, and issued by Superintendent
Plummer on Tuesday, give a total of 15,397
animals affected with the foot and mouth
disease. The number of fresh outbreaks
during the week has been 80, affecting 444

10s. and costs at the Highgate rolicolcourt

A letter from Rome states that a priest
there has just published a collection of the
speeches delivered by the Pope since the 20th
of September, 1870, the date of the overthrow
of the temporal power. The collection fills an
octavo volume of 550 pages. Most of the
speeches are directed against the Italian
Government. The calculation is made that
the Pope in the last two years has spoken at
twenty times greater length than in all the
previous years of his Pontificate.

The Danish Government have declared
Aland to be infected with cholera morbus, and
in consequence all vessels arriving in Danish
ports from that island will be subject to
quarantine inspection.

for the first time. The standards for the

from the China Mail are interesting: "Accom-
modation for reporters for the press is now
provided in the native courts. A number of
children, bought by Chinese for exportation,

an entire family 9f thirteen by native police Is

manufactured at Frankfort, have been put

An interesting service took place in St.
Michael, Wood-street, City, on Sunday morn-
ing, when a collection was made in behalf of
the Metropolitan and City Police Orphanage.
A large number of the police took part in the
singing whioh was of a very congregational
character. The church was crowded through-
out. The sermon was preached by the Rector,
the Rev. R. W. Bush, M.A., and in all a sum
of about £25 was collected for this excellent
institution. This is the first sermon that has
been preached in aid of the Orphanage.

We learn from Cardiff that the American
ship James S. Southard took fire on Monday
morning while lying off the Monkstone, in the
Bristol Channel. It was foutid impossible to
aubdue the flames, and the burning ship was
towed into shallow water, and beached under
Penarth Headland. The masts were cut away,
and the vessel was ultimately. scuttled. The
ship, which was commanded by Captain
tishop, who was also part oWner, was bound
for Callao with a cargo of steam coal. She
was built at Richmond eight years ago.

M. Jules Simon, the Minister of Publie In-
struction in France, has issued a circular in
which he maintains that the dead languages
might, by a better system, be taught in much
less time than at present, and thus enable
students to study modern languages as well.
His principle is that the latter languages are
learned to be spoken, and the former to be
read. M. Simon would accordingly abolish
the system of making Latin verses, and have
the student thoroughly imbued with the best
Latin authors, so that he Might read and enjoy
thorn Alibis life.

tended meeting of the miners of South
Staffordshire and East Worcestershire to con-
sider a proposal to apply to Parliament next
session to incorporate a company to drain the

flames extended, and that in Madrid on Wed-
nesday night fears were entertained that one
of the most magnificent piles of building in

A singular accident, which might have been
attended With disastrous results, occurred on
Wednesday in Rhondda Valley, south Wales,
at the Ton Colliery. In this valley there are 600
men employed, and when the cage was about
to descend to bring the men to bank on Wed-
nesday night the rope broke, and all commu-
nication with the men below was out off.
Some few daring fellows continued to asoend
the shaft at the peril of their lives; but the ma-
jority were content to be entombed in the pit
for the night. A second rope was to have been
rigged on Thursday morning.

The Old Hill magistrates had before them
the case wherein Joseph Fletcher, a miner,
nits charged with having committed an aggra-
vated assault upon his daughter Betsey, aged
14. The assault consisted in chaining the
girl by her legs to a block because she ran
away, and would not work at her trade as a
nailer. He had also also beaten her with a
strap, and had kicked her, causing a wound
upon her back, There was no doubt from the
evidence that the girl was a very bad girl, and
gave much trouble. The magistrates sentenced
the father to three months' imprisonment, with
hard labour.

from the Republican propaganda he initiated

welcome, deputations have waited on him to
explain the condition of local opinion, and then
he has been banquetted for the purpose of
drawing an oration from him.
